title: The basket in the reeds (Exodus 2:1–10)
hook: a mother, a sister watching, and Pharaoh's daughter who pities the child

segments.voice: Yesterday, the midwives: Shiphrah and Puah feared God more than Pharaoh and let the boys live. Your line was two women said no. What small wrong did you refuse? Day three hundred sixty-eight.

Pharaoh's order is out: every Hebrew baby boy goes into the Nile. And in one house of the tribe of Levi, a boy is born. His mother looks at him and sees, the text says, that he's a goodly child. So she hides him. One month. Two. Three. Three months of a newborn: the crying at three in the morning, the neighbors, the thin walls. When she can't hide him any longer, she does something that sounds like obeying the order and is the opposite. She puts her son in the Nile. Just not the way Pharaoh meant.
screen: `EVERY BOY INTO THE NILE.` → `THREE MONTHS OF HIDING.` → `INTO THE NILE, HER WAY.`

segments.voice: First, the basket. She takes a basket of papyrus reeds, seals it with tar and pitch, lays the baby inside, and sets it among the reeds at the river's edge. The Hebrew word for this basket is tevah, the same word Genesis uses for Noah's ark. A boat that carries life through deadly water, again, only this time it's the size of a baby. Second, the sister. She stands at a distance, the text says, to see what will happen. She isn't named here. Later the Bible names Moses's sister as Miriam, and tradition takes her to be this girl. She just watches. Third, Pharaoh's daughter. She comes down to bathe, sees the basket, sends her maid to fetch it, and opens it. The baby is crying. And she has compassion on him, and says, in the Douay-Rheims: "This is one of the babes of the Hebrews." She knows exactly what he is, and whose order he's under. Her father's. And she pities him anyway. Fourth, the sister's move. She steps out of hiding, quick as anything: shall I go and find you a nurse from the Hebrew women? Go, says the princess. And the girl fetches the baby's own mother. Pharaoh's daughter even pays her to nurse her own son. When he's older, the princess adopts him and names him Moses, because, she says, she drew him out of the water. So count the women before Moses says a single word: two midwives, a mother, a sister, a princess. The king's plan was to drown the boys. Every one of those women undid it.
screen: `A TEVAH: THE SAME WORD AS NOAH'S ARK.` · `A SISTER STANDS AT A DISTANCE.` · `ONE OF THE BABES OF THE HEBREWS.` · `DRAWN OUT OF THE WATER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch over someone small. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who can't fully protect themselves: a child, a new neighbor who doesn't speak the language yet, an elderly relative, a kid at school who sits alone. You don't have to rescue anyone today. The sister in the reeds didn't. She just stayed close enough to see, and spoke up at the right moment. Picture that person, and ask where you could stand at a distance and keep watch. If you pray, you can hold them before God by name. If you don't, just keep them in view for these two minutes. The bell holds the time.
Tevah, the Hebrew word for basket, the same one used for Noah's ark: a boat that carried baby Moses through deadly water. Today's word.
Your line: a sister watched. Today, keep an eye out for someone small or overlooked, and be ready to speak up when the moment comes. Day three hundred sixty-eight.

howItsDone: Matthew's Gospel tells of the infant Jesus carried to safety in Egypt when Herod ordered the boys of Bethlehem killed, and Catholic preaching sometimes sets that rescue beside the infant Moses saved from a king's order.

original.note: Hebrew: the basket. Genesis uses the same word for Noah's ark.

trapdoor: what you thought: a sweet story about a baby in a basket.
what it means: a mother, a sister and a princess quietly undo a king's order to drown the boys.
what a scholar hears: tevah links the basket to Noah's ark; the princess ties the name Moses to drawing him out of the water.

sources.quoted: This is one of the babes of the Hebrews.

notes: Tevah used only for Noah's ark (Genesis 6–9) and Moses's basket (Exodus 2:3, 5): standard observation; confirm.
The sister is unnamed in Exodus 2; identified with Miriam by tradition (Numbers 26:59 names Miriam as sister of Moses and Aaron). Confirm.
Exodus 2:6 ('this is one of the Hebrews' children') is KJV wording, used unquoted in the voice; treat as paraphrase or confirm DR wording.
Name Moses: Hebrew wordplay with mashah (to draw out) and the Egyptian element ms/mose (born of, son, as in Thutmose); confirm the trapdoor wording.
